name: Scarcity Principle
description: Limited availability (real or implied) of an option increases its perceived value and desirability.
design_relevance_note: The mechanism behind low-stock warnings, countdown timers, and 'limited time offer' messaging — genuinely effective, and also the specific mechanism most weaponized in dark patterns (see find-dark-patterns-scale).
prevalence_note: One of Cialdini's six core principles; 'only 3 left' / 'selling fast' messaging is one of the most common patterns in e-commerce UX.

findings.description: Meta-analysis of 416 effect sizes from 131 studies finds scarcity cues (demand-based, supply-based, time-based) reliably increase consumer purchase intentions, with the mechanism moderated by product type: demand-based scarcity works best for utilitarian products, supply-based scarcity for experiences, and time-based urgency for high-involvement products.
findings.effect_size: Meta-analytic effect across 416 effect sizes (see paper for category-specific estimates)
findings.source_title: Scarcity tactics in marketing: A meta-analysis of product scarcity effects on consumer purchase intentions

applications.title: Booking.com's urgency messaging, clarified (not eliminated) after EU enforcement
applications.description: Booking.com used urgency phrases like 'last room available!' without disclosing that the claim applied only to Booking.com's own platform, not availability generally. Following a European Commission-led Consumer Protection Cooperation Network enforcement action, Booking.com committed to clarify this scope and to stop presenting offers as time-limited when the same price would still be available afterward -- a narrower remedy than eliminating urgency messaging outright.
applications.ethical_note: This is the most strongly evidenced ethical-risk entry in this round: not a commentator's opinion but a real regulator's finding and a named company's own formal commitment addressing the exact pattern described, even though the remedy is narrower (honest disclosure of scope and timing) than eliminating urgency messaging altogether. It corroborates the Amazon anchoring entry's manipulative_risk grading in this same batch from an independent direction -- two separately sourced entries (US FTC-adjacent commentary for Amazon, EU CPC Network enforcement for Booking.com) landing on the same conclusion about scarcity/urgency-messaging patterns needing real scrutiny, not just clever framing.

applications.title: Creative Market's invitation-only seller pool
applications.description: Creative Market restricts how many sellers can join its marketplace, requiring an invitation rather than open self-service signup -- framed as a supply-side curation mechanism rather than a literal capacity limit.
applications.ethical_note: This is scarcity applied to the supply side (who can sell) rather than the demand side (pressuring a buyer to act now), and NN/g's own framing treats it as a quality-curation mechanism, not an urgency tactic aimed at buyers. It genuinely benefits buyers if it keeps seller quality high, which is a materially different ethical shape than the demand-side scarcity entries elsewhere in this batch -- worth keeping distinct rather than treating 'scarcity' as one uniform risk level regardless of which side of the transaction it's applied to.

applications.title: Groupon's combined time- and quantity-limited deal framing
applications.description: Groupon deal pages present both a countdown on how long a deal remains available and a limited count of remaining items, combining two distinct scarcity signals (time and quantity) on the same offer.
applications.ethical_note: Combining two scarcity signals at once is a stronger urgency push than either alone, and NN/g's article doesn't state whether either constraint (the time window, the remaining count) reflects genuine underlying scarcity for a given deal or is set for effect. Genuine time-limited group-buying offers are a real business model, not inherently deceptive, but stacking both cues together is exactly the kind of pattern this corpus's Dark Patterns & Design Ethics topic treats as needing scrutiny into whether the constraint is real. Graded mixed rather than manipulative_risk because NN/g's article makes no allegation that the specific constraints described are fabricated, unlike the Amazon and Booking.com entries in this same batch.

applications.title: Urban Outfitters' newsletter-first access to new arrivals
applications.description: Urban Outfitters publishes information about new arrivals and promotions first via its email newsletter, making early access to that information itself the scarce resource rather than the product or a time window.
applications.ethical_note: Withholding information from non-subscribers to create scarcity of access (rather than scarcity of the product itself) is a subtler pattern than a countdown timer -- it costs a non-subscriber only delayed information, not a lost opportunity to buy, which is a real ethical difference worth naming rather than lumping in with harder urgency tactics. Still graded mixed rather than user_beneficial because the underlying goal is still to convert curiosity into an email-list opt-in, a real trade the user is making, not a pure convenience.
